title: Canonical database and transaction owner
versioning: This record, contracts/database/erd.json, and contracts/database/benchmark.json share one revision counter, so a decision is cited as DR-0004@<revision>:<decision-id> (for example DR-0004@1:DB2) and a store as DR-0004@<revision>:<store-id>. A change to a decision's store, owning process, or owning leaf, or to an entity's store, partition, or delete behavior, is breaking; adding an entity, a planned table, or a limit is additive. A ratified revision pins the SHA-256 of the ERD, the receipt, their schemas, and the generated ADR, so an unapproved edit fails DR_APPROVAL_STALE.
supersession: A ratified revision is never edited. A leaf that needs another store, transaction owner, or process supersedes this record first: the new revision names DR-0004@<n> in supersedes, gives supersessionReason, and lists per decision whether it is kept or changed. Leaves citing a changed decision go back to blocked until they re-cite; leaves citing an unchanged one keep their citation. An unratified revision can be reverted.
context: Issue #18 (ROUNDS-02-L01). Spec lines cite rounds-review's docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-18-rounds-review-board-design.md. A citation path@62d4eae:L<a>-L<b> is lines at the audited revision; facts about next were read at 6c4a5a3. Alternative A was the starting point because every store next added since R0 already works that way, and the SQLite benchmark (contracts/database/benchmark.json, synthetic data only) decides whether it holds.

securityConsequences.account: No runtime or privilege change here. DB2 and DB4 read the account from the bearer's auth record inside the command's transaction, so no command names its own account, and a record from another account answers like a missing one. Gateway-owned collections lose their REST write rules at each transfer.
securityConsequences.privacy: Rows keep the privacy floor DR-0002 gives them, and the ERD names each entity's partition column and what account deletion does to it. The byte store dedupes within one account only, so whether a file exists never shows across accounts (DB10). The benchmark seeds synthetic data and generates its accounts and passwords per run.
securityConsequences.secret: Credentials appear by name only. No runtime writer uses the superuser; it keeps the bootstrap migration and operator use. Each service identity is a non-superuser auth record with its own secret and an exact-name login guard. #73's keyring encrypts provider keys, and later the byte store's files.
securityConsequences.publicBoundary: #19's command routes sit behind nginx's existing /api/ pass-through to PocketBase: no new port, hostname, or route outside /api/. Each route authorizes the account inside its transaction (DB4), and #19's own PR carries the exposure review. The hook routes only the runner calls stay refused at the public URL, as nginx already refuses the admission, execution, snapshot, and share routes.

decisions.title: Canonical write database
decisions.process: PocketBase (the pocketbase container), the only process that opens pb_data
decisions.decision: Career data has one canonical write database: PocketBase's SQLite file pb_data/data.db, in WAL mode. Canonical records, relations, versions, change sets, audit entries, idempotency results, and the outbox all live in it, so one SQLite transaction covers a command and everything it records. File bytes sit beside it in pb_data/storage (DB10). pb_data/logs.db is PocketBase's request log and never canonical. No other process opens these files while PocketBase runs.

alternatives.option: A second database the runner owns (alternative C)
alternatives.reason: No transaction would cover a command's rows and its history; auth, files, and the containment stores stay in PocketBase.

alternatives.option: Postgres through PocketBase
alternatives.reason: PocketBase runs only on its embedded SQLite (rejected options).

failureModes: One node: a deploy, restart, or crash makes the product unavailable until PocketBase is back (one replica, Recreate).
A full disk stops every write, the audit and outbox rows with them.
A long read transaction, such as a backup's, keeps the WAL from checkpointing, so the WAL grows until it ends.
The live pragmas are journal_mode=pending and synchronous=pending (1 is NORMAL): a process crash loses no commit, but a power or kernel crash can lose the last commits before a checkpoint.
limits: One writer: pending commands per second at saturation with 10 accounts (pending with 1), on one Go scheduler thread standing in for the 500m CPU limit.
The WAL peaked at pending under load, and PocketBase's RSS at pending against the 512Mi limit.
It scales up, not out: no second replica and no second writer.
decisions.consequences: #19 to #23 and every context build on one SQLite file, and throughput is bounded by one writer, which the receipt measures against the floor's load.
decisions.migrationImpact: None. The data already lives here.
decisions.rollbackImpact: Nothing to roll back. A revision that picks another database is a full authority transfer under spec 2699's template, scheduled by #17.

decisions.title: Transaction owner and isolation
decisions.process: the command's gateway hook route, in PocketBase's JSVM
decisions.decision: Each command runs in exactly one runInTransaction that its gateway route owns, and commits or rolls back whole. PocketBase queues all writes and explicit transactions through a single db connection (its v0.22.40 notes), so commands run one at a time and see each other as serial. Every read that decides the outcome (the expected versions, the account check, the invariant checks) goes through the transaction's Dao, never $app.dao(), so it sees the command's own writes and nothing that commits after it. No network call runs inside a transaction: provider calls, renders, and relays run outside and come back as new commands. Batch work (backfills, transfers, purges) commits at most 500 rows per transaction, as #14's migration does.

alternatives.option: Optimistic transactions over several connections
alternatives.reason: PocketBase 0.22 writes on one connection; there is nothing to run concurrently.

alternatives.option: One REST call per record with compensation
alternatives.reason: Not atomic: a failure between calls leaves half a command (rejected options).

failureModes: A slow transaction holds the only writer, and every other command queues behind it; the lock budget bounds it.
A read through $app.dao() inside the callback sees only committed state, so a check can pass on rows the command already changed; #19 lints for it.
A network call inside the callback would hold the writer for the call's whole length; #19 refuses it.
A command that throws after its writes leaves nothing behind (the before-commit failpoint), and its retry with the same command_id commits once.
limits: Lock budget: at the steady rate with 10 accounts the writer is held pending at p50 and pending at p99 per command, and a command waits pending at p99 for it.
Batches of at most 500 rows; the transfer's batches of 30 applications held the writer pending at p99.
decisions.consequences: #19's API is one function per command that takes the transaction's Dao. Throughput falls as hold time grows, so commands stay small and do their slow work outside.
decisions.migrationImpact: None now. #19 builds the gateway on it.
decisions.rollbackImpact: None until #19 ships; after that, a superseding revision.

decisions.title: Gateway placement
decisions.process: PocketBase hook routes; the runner is only ever a caller
decisions.decision: The command gateway is a set of PocketBase hook routes under /api/rounds/commands/, registered as Caller rows in docs/security/server-writes.md. The SPA reaches them through nginx's existing /api/ pass-through, under its 1m body cap; no port, hostname, or route outside /api/ is added. The runner reaches PocketBase only through hook routes, never a collection write. On next it still makes 9 direct collection writes, all with the caller's token: the 7 provider and settings writes in backend/routers/ai.py move behind #73's routes, and the 2 in backend/routers/take_home.py end with #3's PR 4, which makes graded rows server-only. Its share and execution calls already use hook routes. PocketBase 0.22 loads *.pb.js only from the top of pb_hooks (checked on the native binary: a nested file never ran), so each package registers its routes in one top-level <package-id>.pb.js and keeps its code at its DR-0002@2 target path.

alternatives.option: Routes in the runner that call PocketBase's REST API
alternatives.reason: Not atomic, and a second authorization point (rejected options).

alternatives.option: Runner-fronted gateway routes (alternative D)
alternatives.reason: An extra hop and process per command with no gain for commands that need no runner work.

failureModes: A route that doesn't register as a Caller row is an unrecorded writer; #19's registry check fails it.
A gateway-owned collection that keeps a REST write rule is a path around the gateway; DB4 nulls it at each transfer.
Until #73 and #3's PR 4 land, the runner's 9 writes keep going around the gateway with the caller's token.
limits: A command body up to nginx's 1m default under /api/.
Handlers run on PocketBase's pool of JS VMs, and a handler's CPU time inside the transaction adds to the lock hold.
decisions.consequences: #19 builds routes, not a service. Each later context adds its commands as hook routes in its package directory.
decisions.rollbackImpact: Before #19 ships, none. After, moving the gateway is a superseding revision and a route-by-route transfer.

decisions.title: Account authorization
decisions.process: the command's gateway hook route, inside its transaction
decisions.decision: The account is the bearer's auth record, which the route reads inside its transaction; no command body names its account. Each record a command loads and each relation endpoint it writes is checked against that account in the same transaction with #10's predicate (pocketbase/pb_hooks/relation_endpoints.js), and #10's triggers stay as the backstop. Share capabilities keep #11's and #12's checks. #9's collection rules (docs/security/account-scope.v1.json) keep guarding legacy REST writes until each context transfers; the transfer leaf then sets that context's create, update, and delete rules to null, and #21's tables are born with null rules. #1's three writer kinds (Caller, Service, System) are ratified as they stand. Service identities are non-superuser auth collections with an exact-name login guard: execution_service and share_resolvers today, ai_gateway (#73) and dispatcher_service (#22) planned. The gateway never authenticates as the superuser.

alternatives.option: Keep #9's collection rules as the only check
alternatives.reason: Hook routes write through the Dao, which skips collection rules (account-scope's superuser_bypass entry).

alternatives.option: Authorize in the runner before calling PocketBase
alternatives.reason: The check would sit outside the transaction it protects, and a second process would hold the decision.

failureModes: A route that loads a record without the account check would cross accounts; the bench answers another account's id and a missing id with the same 404, and #19 keeps that.
A REST write rule left open on a transferred collection is a second writer; #19's bypass guard checks every gateway-owned collection.
Because Dao writes skip collection rules, the route's own check is the only one on its writes.
limits: One account per command; no command spans accounts.
decisions.consequences: Authorization lives in one place per command, inside the transaction. #172 registers each route's rule in its matrix.
decisions.migrationImpact: None now. Each transfer leaf nulls its context's REST write rules in its own migration.
decisions.rollbackImpact: A transfer's rule change rolls back with that transfer, before its point of no return.

decisions.title: Idempotency store
decisions.decision: Command idempotency uses #1's admission_commands, keyed by its unique (account, command_id) index, with the v7 id check it already enforces. #20 adds domain-command rows kept 30 days; they cascade with the account, and the 30-day expiry bounds that cascade. A replay with the same fingerprint returns the stored result and writes nothing, and a changed body under the same id is a conflict. #22's due-work removes expired rows, and #20 owns the behavior.

alternatives.option: A new idempotency table for domain commands
alternatives.reason: Two stores for one key; admission_commands already has the key, the v7 check, and the cascade.

alternatives.option: No stored result, only a dedupe key
alternatives.reason: A retry couldn't return the original result, so clients couldn't tell a replay from a conflict.

failureModes: A retry after 30 days is a new command; the window is the contract.
Deleting an account cascades its window of rows in one transaction, about 10,000 at the floor (the bench's idempotency seed).
limits: 30 days of rows per account; the receipt's seed holds 10,000 per account, and the replay share of the mix writes nothing.
decisions.consequences: #20 extends a live table instead of adding one, and #19's replay path reads it inside the command's transaction.
decisions.migrationImpact: #20 adds its columns and the domain row kind in an additive migration.
decisions.rollbackImpact: #20's migration has a down step; admission rows are untouched.

decisions.title: Aggregate and version model
decisions.decision: Every aggregate row carries an integer version that each committed change raises by one. A command sends the versions it read as a vector keyed by aggregate id; one stale entry rejects the whole command with the current versions and writes nothing. #19 composes cross-aggregate work, such as a new offer superseding the active one and the opportunity's status following it, as sub-commands of one command in one transaction, each checking and raising its own version. #21's change set log is the default history: one change set per command, with a per-account commit_position assigned in the transaction. Revision tables exist only where a record pins a version (#21).

alternatives.option: Timestamps or ETags instead of integer versions
alternatives.reason: Clock-based checks can tie or skew; an integer per aggregate is exact and cheap to compare.

alternatives.option: A revision row for every write
alternatives.reason: Doubles the write amplification for history the change-set log already keeps.

failureModes: A client holding stale versions gets a conflict with the current ones and must re-read; nothing is half applied.
Two commands on one aggregate serialize on the writer; the second sees the first's version.
limits: The mix writes pending rows per command on average (weighted), counting the record, its change set, audit, outbox, and idempotency rows.
decisions.consequences: #20 owns versions and conflicts, #21 the change-set log, and #19 the composition of sub-commands.
decisions.migrationImpact: Each context's transfer adds its version column; no data changes here.
decisions.rollbackImpact: A context's version column rolls back with its transfer.

decisions.title: Outbox and projectors
decisions.decision: A command writes its domain events to domain_outbox in its own transaction, with #22's library in pocketbase/pb_hooks/lib/revision-audit/. The relay, the job queue, and the due-work tick run in the runner's dispatcher as dispatcher_service and call PocketBase routes under /api/outbox/. With two runner replicas, one consumer stays active through #22's outbox-relay lease in platform_leases: each grant carries a fencing token, and a write under an older token is refused. Projectors apply events in PocketBase transactions and record progress in projector_checkpoints (#23), and outbox_watermarks skips a redelivered event. cronAdd keeps only the sweeps, since its one-minute granularity can't meet a 2 s lag target.

alternatives.option: cronAdd as the relay
alternatives.reason: A one-minute tick can't keep p95 lag under 2 s.

alternatives.option: A relay inside PocketBase hooks after commit
alternatives.reason: Network delivery from a hook would hold a JS VM, and an after-commit hook has no retry or lease.

failureModes: A relay that applies events and dies before its checkpoint redelivers them; the bench's mid-relay failpoint shows they're skipped once.
A relay with a lapsed lease keeps writing; its fencing token is refused (the bench's fenced acks).
A crash after commit and before the relay leaves events in the outbox; the next holder relays them once (the after-commit failpoint).
limits: Relay lag p95 pending at the steady rate with 10 accounts, against 2 s.
Read-your-writes p99 pending through the projection, against 5 s.
decisions.consequences: #22 runs the relay in the runner and #23 the projectors in PocketBase; both write through dispatcher_service.
decisions.migrationImpact: #22 and #23 add their tables in additive migrations with null rules.
decisions.rollbackImpact: Their migrations have down steps; no canonical row depends on a projection.

decisions.title: Backup and restore owner
decisions.store: n/a:a procedure over sqlite-data and files; #157 names the backup target
decisions.process: an operator procedure with a reader process beside PocketBase, owned by #157
decisions.decision: #157 owns backup and restore. The method is an online, SQLite-consistent copy of data.db by a reader (SQLite's backup API, or VACUUM INTO), then the byte store, with file deletes held until the next backup has run. A backup then stops nothing. PocketBase's own backup API zips all of pb_data while holding the writer, and today's procedure (docs/operations.md) stops PocketBase for as long as its tar takes; the receipt measured all three. A restore runs on the same image tag and is verified before traffic returns. docs/operations.md stays as it is until #157 changes it.

alternatives.option: Stop PocketBase and tar pb_data (today)
alternatives.reason: A full outage for the archive's length: pending s at 10 accounts.

alternatives.option: PocketBase's backup API
alternatives.reason: It holds the writer for the whole zip, so every command waits.

failureModes: A file deleted before the backup that last saw it can't be restored; deletes wait for the next backup.
A copy taken mid-write by a plain file copy can be torn; only SQLite's own copy is consistent.
A restore onto another image tag could migrate on first start; restores use the backup's tag.
limits: Restore at 10 accounts: pending s against 30 minutes (pending).
decisions.consequences: #157 writes the procedure and its rehearsal; #76 holds file purges until a backup has run.
decisions.rollbackImpact: The old procedure stays valid until #157 replaces it.

decisions.title: PocketBase retained, upgraded, or replaced
decisions.store: n/a:a binary version, not a store
decisions.decision: Retain PocketBase and stay on its 0.22 line, which upstream still patches. Stage P3 (ROUNDS-02-L01/P3) moves the pin to 0.22.57, the newest 0.22 release, which adds no database migration and changes no hook API. The port to the current major line is deferred until a trigger in the version analysis fires. From #19 on, new hook code reaches PocketBase's API through one module, pocketbase/pb_hooks/lib/pocketbase.js, so that port rewrites one module and the migrations instead of every package.

alternatives.option: Port to the current major line before #19
alternatives.reason: Rewrites all 38 migrations and every containment hook now, for no target the benchmark misses.

alternatives.option: Keep 0.22.22 as pinned
alternatives.reason: Upstream's later 0.22 releases carry its backported fixes; staying behind them buys nothing.

failureModes: Upstream stops publishing 0.22 releases, so later fixes need the port; that is the first trigger.

Upstream archived its GitHub repository on 2026-10-26 and its README points to a new home; the Dockerfile still fetches the release zip from GitHub against its pinned SHA-256, and a build fails rather than take another file.
limits: Every hook and migration on next is written against 0.22's API.
decisions.consequences: P3 is a pin change; the port, when a trigger fires, is its own leaf with the strategy below.
decisions.migrationImpact: None within the 0.22 line. The port's migration plan is in the version analysis.
decisions.rollbackImpact: Within the 0.22 line, roll back by image tag. The port's boundary is in the version analysis.

decisions.title: Byte store
decisions.process: PocketBase file storage, written by gateway routes
decisions.decision: Bytes live in PocketBase's file storage, pb_data/storage, behind one account-scoped collection, account_blobs: one row per stored file, its SHA-256, size, privacy class, and retention metadata, unique on (account_id, sha256). Identical bytes in two accounts are two files. #73's keyring encrypts files once its keys exist, and older files are rewrapped as #22 due-work. #157's backup copies the files after the database, and #76 purges a row, then its file once the next backup has run. #53 (ROUNDS-10-L01) writes it first. #4's snapshot markup files stay where they are and are adopted as they stand. #6's render outputs get a path only: the same collection, written by complete as execution_service, held with the containment release. PocketBase's S3 setting is the path past one disk.
decisions.dedupe: Within one account only. The unique key starts with account_id, and a lookup never reads another account's rows, so uploading bytes can't reveal whether another account holds them.

alternatives.option: A volume outside PocketBase
alternatives.reason: A second store with its own backup and purge, and no transaction tying a row to its file.

alternatives.option: An object store now
alternatives.reason: Self-hosters would need one before they need the scale; PocketBase's S3 setting keeps it a later switch.

failureModes: A file whose row commits but whose write fails leaves a row without bytes; the row is written after the file, and a sweep finds orphans.
Bytes written before #73's keys exist are plaintext until rewrapped.
The disk fills with bytes before rows; the PVC sizing in the storage plan sets the floor.
limits: The 2 GiB sample copied at pending in a restore; 10 GB per account is extrapolated from that rate, labeled so in the receipt.
decisions.consequences: #53, #91, #6, and #4 share one byte store with one dedupe rule and one purge path.
decisions.migrationImpact: #53 adds account_blobs in an additive migration; #4's files are adopted without moving.
decisions.rollbackImpact: #53's migration has a down step while account_blobs is empty; after files land, a forward fix.

alternativesEvaluated.name: PocketBase hook routes owning the transaction
alternativesEvaluated.runnerWritePath: Hook routes only, with the caller's bearer or a service identity, as the runner already does for admission, execution, snapshots, and shares.
alternativesEvaluated.imageBuild: Unchanged: the published PocketBase binary with pb_migrations, pb_hooks, and seeds copied in.
alternativesEvaluated.bindings: None new: hooks are JavaScript in PocketBase's JSVM, and #182's contracts are JSON Schema the SPA, hooks, and runner share.
alternativesEvaluated.nginxChange: None: commands use the existing /api/ pass-through.
alternativesEvaluated.reason: One process and one transaction per command, the pattern every containment store on next already uses; the receipt decides whether it holds.

alternativesEvaluated.name: PocketBase as a Go framework
alternativesEvaluated.runnerWritePath: Go routes in a custom PocketBase build; the runner calls them as in A.
alternativesEvaluated.imageBuild: A CI-built Go binary instead of the published release, rebuilt and re-pinned for every upstream fix.
alternativesEvaluated.bindings: Go types for every command contract, which #182 doesn't generate.
alternativesEvaluated.reason: The same database and transaction model as A, plus a Go toolchain, a custom binary, and a port of every JS hook on next, for nothing the benchmark asks for.

alternativesEvaluated.name: A separate database behind a runner gateway
alternativesEvaluated.runnerWritePath: The runner owns a new database and writes it directly.
alternativesEvaluated.imageBuild: A new database service with its own image, volume, backup, and credentials.
alternativesEvaluated.bindings: Runner models for every aggregate, plus a sync to PocketBase for auth and what stays there.
alternativesEvaluated.nginxChange: Command routes move to runner locations.
alternativesEvaluated.reason: Two authorities: auth, files, and the containment stores stay in PocketBase, so no transaction covers a command that touches both, and every account check crosses the network.

alternativesEvaluated.name: A PocketBase gateway the runner calls as a non-superuser client
alternativesEvaluated.runnerWritePath: The runner forwards each command to gateway hook routes as a service identity, passing the caller's bearer.
alternativesEvaluated.nginxChange: Command routes go to the runner, and the gateway routes are refused at the public URL.
alternativesEvaluated.reason: An extra hop and process per command, and the route must still verify the forwarded bearer. A keeps this shape for the runner's own calls, such as execution completions and provider results.

rejected.reason: Each REST call commits alone, so a command spanning records can stop halfway, which is how the browser invariants break today.

rejected.option: FastAPI writing the SQLite file directly
rejected.reason: A second writer outside PocketBase's write queue that skips its rules, hooks, and realtime events, on a volume only PocketBase mounts.

rejected.option: Postgres through PocketBase, as the k8s comment promised
rejected.reason: PocketBase runs only on embedded SQLite; its FAQ says "there are no plans for supporting other databases".

Goes through pocketbase/pb_hooks/lib/pocketbase.js, so the port changes one module.

breakSites.note: #172 cites this record's pin when it lands.

pocketbase.strategy: Within the 0.22 line (P3): a pin change with no migration, no hook change, and no data change; CI's harness checks the new image. New hook code goes through pocketbase/pb_hooks/lib/pocketbase.js, the only module that calls the Dao, runInTransaction, requestInfo, and the record API. When a trigger fires, the port is its own leaf: each deployment first runs the last 0.22 release, then the new image; fresh installs get a squashed baseline (one current-format snapshot plus the seed, the admin bootstrap, and the JSON size step) that passes #1's migration lint; existing installs keep their _migrations history; and the port re-runs this benchmark on the new version.
pocketbase.freezeWindow: Within the 0.22 line, none: the new binary starts on the same data with no migration. For the port, the new binary's first start, which runs its system migrations over the whole database; the port measures it on a copy at the floor against the 15-minute freeze target. For scale, a startup schema change at 10 accounts here was down pending s.
pocketbase.rollbackBoundary: Within the 0.22 line, roll back by image tag at any time. For the port, roll back by image tag before the new binary's first start; after it, only the pre-upgrade backup, which loses later writes, or a forward fix (spec 2699).
triggers: Upstream stops publishing 0.22 releases with backported fixes.
A fix the deployment needs lands only on the current major line.
A leaf needs a feature only the current major line has.

identifiers.rule: Existing collections keep user as the partition column, logically account_id and set by the server once #9's rules ship; #24 and #159 decide any rename. Platform tables (#21 to #23) use indexed, non-cascading account_id text, because a 50,000-row cascade would hold the single writer, and #76 purges them in batches. #1's and #3's stores keep their cascading relations as built, and #20's idempotency rows cascade, bounded by their 30-day expiry.

Account data has opaque ids the server makes; a client never picks a canonical id. Content is keyed by (pack, track, slug, content version). Slugs become aliases through #156's redirect table (slug_redirects), which replaces both slug paths at 62d4eae: getApplication's slug match and the mention index's title slugs.

A command_id is a UUIDv7 that #19's SPA client makes per user action. Other actors and #22's retries derive a UUIDv7-shaped id: the 48-bit time of the source event or job, then 74 bits of SHA-256 over actor kind, handler or consumer name, source id, and effect index. #124's registered effects hash system and the effect key, timed by the first EffectArmed, so a re-arm reuses the id. No id hashes the attempt number, and every id passes #19's v7 check and #20's 30-day window. The bench's derivedId implements this rule and its test checks it against Python's.

#44's kinds are stored as: instant, a UTC date field plus an IANA zone in text; local datetime, floating ISO text; calendar date and all-day, YYYY-MM-DD text, never a date field; partial date, ISO text at its precision plus an approximate flag or unknown, with a sort key; duration, integer minutes.

invariants.detail: Creating an offer supersedes the active one, and deleting it revives the prior one, in one command. A partial unique index allows one active offer per opportunity, so two concurrent creates can't both commit.
The status change that follows an offer is a sub-command of the offer's command, with its own expected version, instead of a whole-row write from page state.
The account bootstrap command creates the Default campaign if it is absent, inside one transaction, and the unique (user, slug) index backs it (line 299 of the init migration at 62d4eae).

The browser creates pairs one call at a time, and the pair index leaves out user (1700003000_experience_connections.js, lines 42 to 59 at 62d4eae). A pair becomes unique per account, on (user, parent, child), with #10's checks and triggers on both ends, and a merge repoints pairs inside the merge's transaction.
